title: The peace chant — purnam adah, purnam idam — from fullness, fullness (5.1)
hook: light a candle from a candle and the first flame loses nothing: the great line we leave the Brihadaranyaka on, chanted all over the world
tomorrow: the teacher's charge to the student: "speak the truth, practice dharma"

segments.voice: Yesterday, neti, neti: not this, not this, and Yajnavalkya finally went away. Did you answer not this to a job, a mood or a mistake? Day three hundred eighty-eight.

Light a candle. Now use it to light a second one. Look at the first flame. It hasn't gotten any smaller. Light ten more from it, a hundred, and it's still exactly as bright. Something was given away completely, and nothing was lost. If you've ever been to a Hindu gathering, a yoga class, or the start of an Upanishad recital, you may have heard a short chant in Sanskrit that ends om shanti, shanti, shanti. Many people know the sound. Fewer know it comes from the Brihadaranyaka, at the opening of its fifth book, as we reach the end of our time in it.
screen: `A CANDLE LIGHTS A CANDLE.` → `THE FIRST FLAME LOSES NOTHING.` → `A CHANT MANY PEOPLE KNOW BY SOUND.`

segments.voice: Here it is. Purnam adah purnam idam purnat purnam udacyate, purnasya purnam adaya purnam evavashishyate. That is full. This is full. From the full, the full comes forth. Take the full from the full, and the full alone remains. Purna means full, whole, complete, lacking nothing. That is the far side, Brahman beyond everything you can point to. This is the near side, the world right here, the one you're sitting in. And the chant refuses to make either one the lesser half. The world doesn't come out of Brahman like a slice out of a cake, leaving a hole. It comes out like a flame from a flame. People who love mathematics sometimes hear infinity in it: take infinity from infinity, and infinity is left. The tradition attaches it as the peace chant of the Isha Upanishad, too, and it's chanted at the start of study, worship and gatherings. And it's a fitting place to finish the Brihadaranyaka. Look back down this great forest of a book. The horse that was the whole cosmos. Death's hunger making a world. The breath the demons couldn't pierce. I am, then fear, then longing. The self split into two halves. Maitreyi setting aside the earth. Salt with no inside or outside. Honey for each other. A thousand cows, eight challengers, a head that fell. The light of the self, the dreamer, deep sleep, the caterpillar, desire. Not this, not this. And at the end, not emptiness. Fullness. Tomorrow, a new Upanishad, the Taittiriya, and a teacher's speech to his graduating students.
screen: `THAT IS FULL. THIS IS FULL.` · `A FLAME FROM A FLAME, NOT A SLICE.` · `THE PEACE CHANT OF STUDY AND WORSHIP.` · `THE WHOLE FOREST OF A BOOK.` · then, large: `FULL FROM FULL.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of fullness. Sit, and breathe. On the in-breath, let the word come: full. On the out-breath: full. Notice the breath you just gave away left you lacking nothing; the next one is already arriving. If you'd like, say the chant silently, or just its first line: purnam adah, purnam idam. Let the line and the breath move together until the words fall away. The bell holds the time.
Purna. Full, whole, complete. In the peace chant, what that is, what this is, and what remains when the full is taken from the full.
Your line: full from full. Today, give something away completely, time, attention, a good word, and notice whether you're any less. Day three hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: The purnam adah chant is recited as the shanti mantra of the Isha Upanishad and of the Shukla Yajurveda tradition, at the start and end of study, at pujas and at many gatherings, followed by om shanti, shanti, shanti.

the chant says the world is a lesser part cut off from Brahman
that is full, this is full: a flame from a flame, not a slice from a cake.
taking the full from the full leaves nothing, the chant says

fork.setup: you take the full from the full. what's left?
fork.reveal: purnam evavashishyate: the full alone remains. like a flame that lights a hundred others and stays just as bright.

original.note: Sanskrit pūrṇam: full, whole, complete. pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam, that is full, this is full.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty chant to start a yoga class.
what it means: that and this, the beyond and the world, are both whole, and giving one from the other loses nothing.
what a scholar hears: Brihadaranyaka 5.1.1, also the śānti-pāṭha of the Isha Upanishad; Shankara reads 'that' as the unmanifest and 'this' as the manifest.

sources.quoted: purnam adah purnam idam purnat purnam udacyate, purnasya purnam adaya purnam evavashishyate

notes: Closes the Brihadaranyaka run (days 360–388); the look-back recaps days 360–387. Adjust if any were written differently. Books 5–6 (e.g., the thunder's da da da, 5.2) are outside the outline.

Use as the Isha Upanishad's shanti mantra and in the Shukla Yajurveda tradition: confirm.
